zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical review aid: [Entry Words Data of Nippojisho](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, licensed [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Consulted after independent visual reading; the scan governs this transcription.

lines.note: Lugem completes fu-lugem from f459; the preceding page's catchword anticipates this row. Susuhaki names soot removal. The scan prints felugẽ, without the extra i introduced by OCR, and retains its historical first vowel.
The alternative Portuguese gloss is sweeping the soot from a house. Eſfolinhar is retained as printed rather than modernized.
Susubana is the moisture or discharge running from the nose. The entry is distinct from the preceding soot compound despite the shared initial letters.
Susubana wo tarasu means letting nasal discharge drip. Pollos and the printed division nari- / zes are retained.

runs.text: zes eſte humor como quando hum tẽ catarro.

lines.note: Zes completes narizes; the gloss compares the discharge with that of a person suffering a cold. Tẽ is the printed abbreviated verb.
Susudoi describes someone very judicious and shrewd. Muito prudente replaces the draft Muto pradente; the qualification of severity follows below.
The acuity is accompanied by rigor or harshness. Item introduces another sense rather than another Japanese headword.
Valẽte and brioſo give the further sense of being brave and spirited. The abbreviation tilde in Valẽte is kept.
Susudô is the corresponding adverbial form. The upward circumflex is clearly printed and is not substituted with a caron.
Susudosa is the nominal derivative, expressing the quality just described. The separate short line is intentional.
Susuhaki cross-refers to susu, whose extended entry began on f459. Vide is italic, whereas the cited Japanese ſuſu is roman.
Susugi means rinsing or washing. The Portuguese second verb is lauar, with l rather than the OCR t; the printed principal parts are not expanded.
Kuchi wo susugu is rinsing the mouth. The Portuguese lauar and enxaguar provide near-synonymous explanations whose object follows below.
Boca completes the mouth example. The figurative haji wo susugu means washing away dishonor; Vin- begins the Portuguese explanation of avenging oneself.

Completes vingar-se and adds freeing oneself from an affront. Mimi wo susuida introduces ears that have been figuratively washed; the repeated m and the final i before the visible hyphen correct the draft.

runs.text: Se diz quando hum folgou de ouuir al-

lines.note: Da completes susuida, the past form. The expression is used when someone enjoys hearing a good discourse; the Portuguese al- continues algũa.

runs.text: gũa pratica, ou prègação boa com que pa-

lines.note: Gũa completes algũa. A good discourse or sermon is what the listener enjoyed; prègação retains the accent of the supplied reading, and pa- continues parece.

runs.text: rece que lauou, ou purificou os ouuidos.

lines.note: Rece completes parece: it seems the discourse has washed or purified the ears. This explains the metaphor in mimi wo susuida, not literal ear washing.
Susume is the noun persuasion or encouragement. The following separately printed entry supplies the corresponding verb.
Susume means persuading or urging. Ienuo here is zen wo, virtue as the object of encouragement; the initial I is the dictionary's consonantal spelling, not an anomalous vowel sequence.

runs.text: Exortar, ou mouer a alguem à

lines.note: Susumuru completes zen wo susumuru, exhorting someone to virtue. The Portuguese Exortar and mouer explain the inducement, whose goal continues below.
After virtue, sake wo susumuru introduces urging someone to drink. The scan supports ſuſumuru without the draft's extra r; Perſua- continues persuadir.

runs.text: dir a alguem que beba vinho. ¶

lines.note: Dir completes persuadir: inducing someone to drink wine. Kore xo- begins a new example about something stimulating the appetite.
Cuuo completes xocuuo, the food/appetite expression with the object particle. Both u types are visible. The sentence says that this stimulates appetite; the printed monogia is retained.
Vontade de comer completes the appetite gloss. Uma wo susu- begins the example of urging a horse forward.
Muru completes susumuru, with susume yaru as the alternative. The Portuguese begins making the horse walk or run.
Correr o caualo completes the horse example. The row is a short continuation, not a separate entry.

Susumi is the corresponding self-directed or intransitive verb: impelling oneself, being persuaded, or advancing. The damaged Portuguese In iterſe is retained; Inciterſe is a likely reading, but the lost internal type is not securely visible.

runs.text: fazer algũa couſa, ou ir a diante. Vt,

lines.note: The action is doing something or going forward. Ien- again begins zen, virtue, in an example completed on the next row.

runs.text: Incitarſe à virtude, ou ir adiã-

lines.note: Zen ni susumu is impelling oneself toward virtue or advancing in it. The clearly printed Incitarſe gives a semantic comparator for the damaged word on c1-l028; adiã- continues adiante.
Te completes adiante. Shoku ga susumu is then illustrated as having an appetite; the grammatical subject differs from the transitive example above.
Vontade de comer completes the appetite gloss. It closes the susumi entry before the compounds that follow.
Susumichikazuku is advancing closer, directly glossed as coming near. The repeated z spelling is preserved as printed.
Susumiide means stepping out or coming forward. Sair, not Suir, matches the visible a and the explanation continued below.
The person comes forward without being called. This is an indented continuation of susumiide, not an independent entry; the draft also misread sair as saur.
Susumiyuki is proceeding onward. Its Portuguese manner phrase continues with fervor below; the printed abbreviated yuita remains unchanged.
Feruor supplies the zeal or ardor of proceeding. The rounded damaged vowel is o, not the draft a of feruar.
Susuqe describes becoming smoky or soot-darkened, illustrated by a house. The ending quru is retained as a historical principal form.
The alternative is becoming blackened and old. Fazerſe corrects fazorſe; goei ga begins an example with an image as its subject.

runs.text: A imagem està ja muito defuma-

lines.note: Susuqeta completes the statement that the image has become soot-darkened. Defuma- continues the Portuguese adjective across the row boundary.
Da completes defumada, paired with velha. This closes the smoky-image example rather than describing the grass in the next entry.

runs.text: Certa erua de que fazem vaſouras, eſ-

lines.note: Susuki is described as an herb or grass used to make brooms. The gloss continues with mats; it does not itself specify a scientific species name.
Teiras completes esteiras, mats, another use of the grass. The short continuation remains a separate row.

runs.text: Lugar õde nace muita deſta erua.

lines.note: Susukiwara is a place where much of the preceding grass grows. The headword ends vara, not vata; õde abbreviates onde, and the scan prints nace rather than the OCR nare.
Susuri means sipping or sucking. The initial is a worn capital S, not lowercase b; sutta retains the visible doubled t.
Kayu wo susuru means sipping rice gruel, rendered soruer canja. The Japanese object particle remains attached in Cayuuo.

runs.text: Certa laya de peças de ſeda teſa, & crùa.

lines.note: The scan prints Suſuri with r for a type of stiff raw-silk cloth; it is not silently changed to expected Suſuxi. The supplied NINJAL headword notes also identify this as a printed error. Second-pass enlargement confirms a grave on crùa. The row is an independent headword, not an indented continuation.
Suta means many, exemplified by suta no hito, many people. The abbreviated Portuguese homẽs retains its tilde.
Sutabi means many times, with Sudo recommended as the better form. Meliùs is wholly italic, with a grave over u; the draft's alternating roman fragments were spurious.
Sutaka is a falcon taken from its nest. The gloss describes how the bird is obtained rather than a separate zoological species.
Sutameki means breathing or panting with effort. The scan ends this clause with a comma, joining the fatigue description below.
The labored breathing is accompanied by weariness or fatigue. Both Portuguese nouns continue the preceding definition.
Sutaqi has the same meaning, as indicated by Idem. Its principal parts are kept in their abbreviated printed form.
Sutakiayeki again describes labored breathing, now elaborated as noisy panting. Trabalho has a visible initial t, omitted by the draft.

runs.text: & fadiga, fazendo estrondo com a voz.

lines.note: The panting involves fatigue and an audible noise of the voice. Fadiga corrects faciga; the provisional short-s reading of estrondo is retained rather than globally reclassifying the ligature.
Sutare means worsening or falling into disrepair. The scan has Sutare, not Suatare, and danificarſe retains the small i missing from the OCR.
Sutarehate intensifies the preceding verb: becoming thoroughly damaged or ruined. The long s in Acabarſe and the missing i of danificar correct the draft; the final comma is visible.
After the alternative arruinar, the example describes the capital's condition in recent years. Qinnen ends in n, not u; yo- begins yorozu on the next row.

Rozzu completes yorozu: everything has fallen into ruin. Abrasion broke ſutare into misleading OCR fragments; the spacing before fateta is retained. Mon. is an upright citation label before the italic translation.

runs.text: do Miyaco de poucos annos pera cà todas eſtão

lines.note: The translation says that all the capital's affairs have deteriorated over the last few years. Annos and eſtão replace malformed OCR strings. Miyaco is a Japanese place designation within the Portuguese sentence.
The capital's affairs are disrupted and destroyed. The surviving b and the ending uidas support desbaratadas and deſtruidas, rather than the draft's corrupted alternatives.

runs.text: Hum liquor que ſe faz do trigo, & fei-

lines.note: Sutate is a liquid seasoning made from wheat and beans. Fei- starts feijões; the description should not be silently replaced with a modern product name.

runs.text: jões, que ſerue muito em Iapão pera temperar o

lines.note: Jões completes feijões. The seasoning is much used in Japan to season food; pera is one word, and Iapão remains Portuguese, not a Japanese font-toggle term.
Comer is the food being seasoned, and dar sabor explains the liquid's purpose. This completes the condiment entry.
Sutçu denotes a bale or sack, here of rice. Fardo and arroz replace Farlho and arrez; the Japanese u is unaccented, unlike the next headword.
Sutçǔ means many letters or written documents. The caron over u distinguishes it graphically from the preceding sack entry.

runs.text: Vento Sul que ventade maneira que

lines.note: Sutebaye is a south wind whose manner of blowing indicates that it will soon stop. The close spacing in ventade is retained from the aligned draft.
The wind is about to end. Kono kaze sutebaye begins the illustrative assertion, completed by de gozaru below.

runs.text: Eſte vento Sul logo ha de ceſ-

lines.note: De gozaru completes the Japanese assertion. The Portuguese says this south wind will soon cease; the worn vowel supports ceſ- rather than the broken c ſ- of the draft.

runs.text: ſar ſegundo o modo de ventar.

lines.note: ſar completes ceſſar. The prediction is based on the wind's manner of blowing, closing the definition of sutebaye.
Sute means throwing away or casting off. The row ends with deſi and a period, not deſ-: there is no lost continuation between this entry and Sutebuchi.

runs.text: Vara com que dão no caualo por de

lines.note: Sutebuchi refers to striking a horse with a rod from behind. The Portuguese prints caualo, not cauaſo; por de continues the directional phrase below.
The blow is given from behind when in haste. The example begins sutebuchi wo utte; the initial S and doubled t are visible, replacing Du ebuchiuo vte. The printed close trasem is retained.

runs.text: Dando com a vara nas ancas do ca-

lines.note: Nigueta says that the rider fled after the blow. The Portuguese locates the rod's strike on the horse's hindquarters and divides caualo after ca-.
Ualo completes caualo, and fugio gives the rider's flight. The horse is not feminine cauala, as the draft implied.
Sutebune is a discarded vessel already hauled ashore or stranded. The headword and Embarcação, eſta, and varada are recoverable from the scan, unlike the OCR fragments.
The vessel is no longer useful for anything. This completes the abandoned-boat description; the provisional st typography in presta remains unchanged.
Sutego is an abandoned or foundling child, glossed criança engeitada. The historical Portuguese spelling is preserved.
Sutemuchi refers back to Sutebuchi. Vide is italic; the Japanese cross-reference is roman and belongs to the explanatory apparatus.

Suwa and suwaya are exclamations of surprise. Eſpãto contains p, not the draft's second long s. The faint grave-like mark over the first u is retained provisionally; it must not force a long-vowel interpretation of the exclamation.

runs.text: Suua core coſo vochǔto naretote. Taif.

lines.note: The quoted suwa exclamation identifies someone as a fugitive. The worn vochǔto is retained as printed rather than normalized to a modern ochiudo form; Taif. is the upright citation label, with its book number below.

runs.text: Lib. 28. O que eſte certo he homẽ q̃ vẽ fugido.

lines.note: Book 28 accompanies the citation. The Portuguese identifies the man as one who has come in flight; vẽ, not oẽ, is the abbreviated verb. The visible terminal period closes the quotation.
Suwabuki denotes a cough, with shiwabuki explicitly preferred. Potiùs is italic, while l and the cited Japanese alternative are roman; the accented u is preserved.
Suwabuki wo suru means coughing or having a cough. The Portuguese single-s spellings Toſir and toſe are not modernized to double s.
Suwai here means small branches or rods from a tree. This botanical noun is distinct from the homonymous brokerage entry below.

runs.text: Officio de corretor entre os que comprão,

lines.note: The second Suwai denotes the work of a broker between purchasers and sellers. Corretor is the commercial intermediary, not a textual corrector.
Vendem completes the buyer-and-seller pair. Suwai wo suru means performing the broker's work; the scan does not show the draft's comma after Fazer.

runs.text: este officio de corretor. ¶ Item, Corretagẽ

lines.note: Completes the brokerage-work example. Item introduces the further sense of brokerage commission; Corretagẽ retains its abbreviation.

runs.text: ou ganho que ſe tira deſte officio. Vt,

lines.note: The further sense is the gain obtained from this occupation. Suwai begins the example of taking the fee, completed below.
Suwai wo toru means taking brokerage or commission. The object particle is uo, not no; Tomar replaces Temar. The final dã- continues the phrase concerning the merchants.
Tre completes the abbreviated dã-tre expression: commission obtained from between the merchants. The historical contraction is preserved rather than rewritten.

runs.text: Feição com certas aberturas, ou en-

lines.note: Suwama describes a shape or pattern with openings, explained through river mouths and inlets. The Portuguese en- continues entradas.

runs.text: tradas de rio, ou enſeadas a que ſe arremeda

lines.note: Tradas completes entradas. River inlets or coves provide the model being imitated; enſeadas and arremeda correct the OCR, and the spurious l after que is removed.

runs.text: nas Niuas, ou nas pinturas dos veſtidos.

lines.note: The inlet-like form is imitated in gardens or garment designs. Niuas is a Japanese garden term embedded in Portuguese; pinturas and veſtidos correct the draft's malformed words. The example continues on f461, anticipated by the catchword.

zones.label: Bottom-right catchword
zones.note: The roman catchword has a paragraph mark and a terminal dot. It anticipates Suuama nari on f461; no hyphen is supplied.
